questions.q: An order.created handler throws. What does await bus.publishEvent(...) do with @zudojs/events in its default settings?
questions.explain: The default error mode is CONTINUE: every handler runs, failures are collected, and the promise resolves. That is why code that only awaits publishEvent, such as a naive relay, never notices a failed delivery. Check result.failed, or log in onError.
options: It rejects with the handler's error, so the caller's try/catch sees it
It resolves; the other handlers still run and the failure is only in result.errors (and the bus's onError hook)
It retries the failing handler three times, then rejects
It stops at the failing handler and resolves with handled: false

questions.q: In the first example, publishing order.created a second time fixed the missing receipt but doubled the revenue. What is the root cause?
questions.explain: Re-publishing runs every subscriber again. Handlers that apply their effect every time they run (append a row, add to a total) double it. The fix has two parts: retry per consumer, and make each consumer ignore events it already handled.
options: The event bus delivered the second event twice
The revenue handler used += on a number instead of a BigInt
A retry was done by re-publishing the whole event, and the audit and analytics handlers were not idempotent
The email handler changed the payload before analytics read it

questions.q: ShopFlow commits the order row, then the process is killed before publishEvent runs. With only an in-memory event bus, what happens to the receipt, audit and analytics work?
questions.explain: The event only existed in memory. The order is committed, and nothing anywhere says "announce this order". The outbox fixes this by writing the event in the same transaction as the order.
options: The bus replays the event when the process restarts
It is lost: nothing recorded that the event still has to be published
The database rolls back the order, so nothing is inconsistent
The handlers run anyway, because they were subscribed before the crash

questions.q: Which of these is not a way the same event can reach a consumer twice?
questions.explain: The first three are everyday causes of duplicates, which is why delivery is "at least once". A unique constraint is part of the defence: it lets the database decide which delivery claimed the event first.
options: The relay publishes a row, then crashes before marking it as published
The queue retries a job that was slow, while the first try is still running
A broker redelivers a message whose acknowledgement was lost
A UNIQUE constraint on the processed_events table

questions.q: Why does bus.on<Event<OrderCreated>>("payment.failed", handler) compile?
questions.explain: The name is a plain string at runtime and the type argument is chosen by the caller, so nothing ties them together. The handler then reads fields that do not exist. Let a contract choose both the name and the type, and parse the payload before the handler runs.
options: Because payment.failed and order.created share a namespace
Because the type argument of on is not connected to the event name; it only describes what the handler claims to receive
Because TypeScript checks event names only when strict is off
Because @zudojs/events converts the payload to the requested type at runtime

questions.q: Who should own and change the order.created contract module?
questions.explain: The producer owns the event, just as a module owns its public API. Consumers import the same contract instead of redeclaring it, so a change shows up in their code review and their compiler.
options: Each consumer keeps its own copy and changes it when it needs a new field
The orders module, which publishes the event; consumers import the contract, and changes are reviewed with the consumer teams
Nobody: contracts are generated from whatever the producer happens to send
The analytics team, because it reads the most fields

questions.q: Which change to order.created needs a new version?
questions.explain: A consumer written for the old shape reads payload.email and gets undefined. Adding an optional field is not breaking: tolerant readers ignore fields they do not know.
options: Adding an optional couponCode field that consumers may ignore
Moving email into a nested customer object
Adding a new consumer that subscribes to the event
Fixing a typo in the documentation comment of the contract

questions.q: A developer wants to change totalKobo to hold naira instead of kobo, keeping the name and type (number). Why is this the most dangerous kind of change?
questions.explain: A change of meaning is invisible to every check that only looks at shape. Give it a new version or, better, a new field name such as totalNaira, so old code cannot mistake one for the other.
options: Numbers cannot be stored in jsonb
The parser will reject every new event
The type and field are unchanged, so neither the compiler nor the parser notices, and every consumer silently computes amounts 100 times too small
Naira values need BigInt, which JSON cannot represent

questions.q: Why does the lesson upcast v1 events when a consumer reads them, instead of converting them once when v2 is deployed?
questions.explain: Events live in many places: unrelayed outbox rows, jobs waiting for a retry, dead letters replayed next week, a broker's log. Converting at read time handles all of them the same way, and the stored events stay a true record of what was published.
options: Upcasting is faster when it runs many times
Old events are already in flight (in the outbox, queues and dead letters) and may be read long after the deploy; you cannot rewrite all of them
PostgreSQL cannot update jsonb columns
The event bus refuses to deliver events whose version changed

questions.q: The v1 → v2 upcaster sets customer.name to null. Why not a friendly default such as "Customer"?
questions.explain: An upcaster may only add what it can derive. Unknown data becomes an explicit "unknown" (null here), and the v2 contract allows it, so consumers are forced to handle it, as the email consumer does with "Hello".
options: Because null is shorter in JSON
Because TypeScript does not allow string defaults in upcasters
Because v1 never recorded the name; an invented value would look like real data in every email and report built on these events
Because the email consumer crashes on strings it did not expect

questions.q: A consumer that knows up to v2 receives a v3 order.created. What does the lesson's readOrderCreated do, and why?
questions.explain: Parsing a newer version as an older one might work by luck, or silently lose a field that matters. Refusing makes the problem loud and recoverable. The usual order of deployment is: consumers first, producers last.
options: It parses the payload as v2 and ignores unknown fields
It downcasts v3 to v2 with a reverse upcaster
It throws, so the job fails and is retried; once the consumer with v3 support is deployed, the retry succeeds
It drops the event, because a newer version is always a mistake

questions.q: ShopFlow adds order.created v3. Which upcasters exist afterwards?
questions.explain: Upcasters form a chain, one version step each. Every new version adds exactly one function, and all older versions reach the latest by running the steps in order.
options: One function from v1 to v3, replacing the v1 → v2 one
The existing v1 → v2 and a new v2 → v3; a v1 event goes through both
Only v2 → v3, because v1 events are too old to matter
None: v3 consumers read every version natively

questions.q: Why must the INSERT INTO outbox run in the same database transaction as INSERT INTO orders?
questions.explain: Two separate commits leave a gap where a crash creates exactly the inconsistency the outbox exists to prevent. One transaction closes the gap.
options: Because PGlite allows only one statement per transaction
So the relay can read the order row
So they commit together or not at all: there is never an order without its event, or an event about an order that was rolled back
So the event id can be generated by the database

questions.q: A relay publishes each outbox row with await bus.publishEvent(...) and then marks it published, without looking at the result. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: In CONTINUE mode publishEvent resolves even when a handler threw. The relay must check result.failed and leave the row unpublished (and stop, to keep the order) when it is greater than zero.
options: Nothing: publishEvent rejects when a subscriber fails, so the UPDATE is skipped
A row is marked published even when a subscriber failed to accept it, so that delivery is lost for good
Every row is published twice
Rows are published in the wrong order

questions.q: A consumer does SELECT from processed_events, then the work, then INSERT into processed_events. Two deliveries of the same event arrive together. Why can the work happen twice?
questions.explain: That is the check-then-act race. The primary key stops the second INSERT, but only after the work was done. Claim first with INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, so the database decides the winner.
options: Because SELECT does not see rows in jsonb columns
Both deliveries can run their SELECT before either inserts, so both see "not processed" and both do the work
Because the primary key is on event_id only
Because PGlite runs queries in parallel threads

questions.q: In handleOnce, why is the claim row inserted in the same transaction as the work?
questions.explain: A claim committed without its work would make the event look done when it is not, and the retry would skip it forever. Work committed without its claim would be repeated by the next delivery. Only committing them together is correct.
options: To make the query faster
If the work fails, the claim is rolled back too, so a retry may try again; if both commit, later deliveries are duplicates
So that other consumers can see the claim before the work finishes
Because ON CONFLICT only works inside a transaction

questions.q: Sending an email cannot be part of a database transaction. What is the best protection against a duplicate email when the consumer crashes between sending and recording?
questions.explain: The event id is the same on every delivery, which makes it a perfect idempotency key. Recording the claim first and never retrying turns a crash into a lost email instead.
options: Send the email twice on purpose, so the customer always gets at least one
Record the claim before sending, and never retry
Pass the event id as an idempotency key to the mail provider, so it drops the repeat send
Put the email in an afterRollback hook

questions.q: Why does each consumer get its own queue, instead of the relay re-publishing the event until every handler succeeds?
questions.explain: Retry state belongs to a consumer, not to an event. The bus handler only enqueues, which is fast and rarely fails; the queue does the slow, unreliable work with retries for that consumer alone.
options: Queues are faster than the event bus
Each consumer then has its own retries, backoff and dead letters: a failing email is retried alone, without running audit and analytics again
Because @zudojs/events cannot have more than one handler per event
So that consumers can change the event payload

questions.q: Which failure should the email consumer park in the dead-letter table at once, instead of throwing for a retry?
questions.explain: A mailbox that does not exist will not start existing after a backoff. Retrying only delays the alert. Timeouts, 429s and reset connections are transient, and the queue's retries are the right answer.
options: The mail provider timed out
The provider answered 429 Too Many Requests
The provider says the mailbox does not exist
The database connection was reset while recording the claim

questions.q: The replay in the lesson clears published_at on the outbox row instead of calling the email handler directly. What is the main benefit?
questions.explain: A replay tool that skips the normal path skips the checks you rely on. Because every consumer is idempotent, re-publishing is safe: audit and analytics answer duplicate, and email does its job.
options: It is the only way to delete a dead letter
The event goes through exactly the same path as the first time (relay, queue, upcaster, parser, idempotency), and idempotent consumers ignore what they already did
It sends the email faster
It gives the event a new id, so it is not treated as a duplicate

questions.q: Before accepting an order, the orders module needs to know whether a product is in stock. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: Events announce facts to whoever cares; they do not return answers. When one module needs an answer to continue, it asks: a query, an RPC call or a function call.
options: Publish stock.check-requested and wait for an event back
A query (or a direct call) to the catalog, because orders needs an answer now
A dead-letter table
An upcaster

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In the default CONTINUE mode the second handler still runs, and the publish resolves. The result counts one success and one failure, and each error carries the handlerId you gave the handler.
options:
audit row written
true 1 1 email
Error: mail provider timed out
true 0 1 email

audit row written
false 1 1 email

questions.q: The same bus, published in the THROW error mode. What does this print?
questions.explain: In THROW mode the first failing handler rejects the publish, wrapped in an EventHandlerError, and the handlers after it do not run. It suits tests and places where every handler must succeed, not a fan-out to independent consumers.
options:
rejected: EventHandlerError
ran: []

rejected: Error
ran: [ 'audit' ]
ran: [ 'audit' ]

rejected: EventHandlerError
ran: [ 'audit' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The type argument is a claim that nothing checks. The payload has amountKobo, not totalKobo, so the handler reads undefined, and no error is raised. A parser at the edge would have refused the payload with a clear message.
options: refund: undefined
refund: 500000
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
Nothing, because the payload does not match the type

questions.q: Deliveries arrive with duplicates. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two deliveries repeat an id already seen, so they are skipped. The three distinct events add up to 400,000 kobo. In a real consumer the Set is the processed_events table, written in the same transaction as the revenue.

questions.q: This consumer checks, then waits (as a database call would), then marks. Two deliveries of the same event arrive together. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both calls pass the check before either has marked the event, because the mark happens after an await. That is the check-then-act race. The cure is an atomic claim, such as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING, before the work.
options: [ 'done', 'done' ] 2
[ 'done', 'duplicate' ] 1
[ 'duplicate', 'duplicate' ] 0
[ 'done', 'duplicate' ] 2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A v1 payload runs through both steps: 1 → 2 moves the email into customer, 2 → 3 adds the channel. A v4 event is refused before the loop starts, instead of being guessed at.
options:
ada@shop.ng null unknown
v4 is newer than v3

ada@shop.ng null undefined
v4 is newer than v3

undefined null unknown
v4 is newer than v3

ada@shop.ng null unknown
TypeError: upcasters[v] is not a function

questions.q: A relay stops at the first row a subscriber refuses. What does this print?
questions.explain: Row 1 is published, row 2 fails and the loop stops, so row 3 is not attempted even though it would have worked. That keeps events in their original order. The next run publishes rows 2 and 3.
options:
1 [ 'evt-ORD-2', 'evt-ORD-3' ]
2 []

0 [ 'evt-ORD-1', 'evt-ORD-2', 'evt-ORD-3' ]
3 []

questions.q: Claims are keyed by consumer and event id. What does this print?
questions.explain: Audit having handled evt-1 says nothing about analytics, so the key includes the consumer. Only the repeat for audit is refused.
options: true true false 2
true false false 1
true true true 3
false true false 2

questions.q: A handler tries to "fix" the payload before the next handler sees it. What does this print?
questions.explain: Handlers receive a frozen copy of the payload. The assignment throws in the higher-priority handler (modules are strict), the bus records the failure and carries on, and analytics sees the original total. One handler cannot change what the next one sees.
options:
analytics sees 2500000
failed: 1

analytics sees 0
failed: 0

analytics sees 2500000
failed: 0
TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'totalKobo' of object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only failures known to be permanent are parked. Everything else, including an error without a code, is retried: an unknown error might be temporary, and after the last attempt the queue dead-letters it anyway.
options: retry park retry retry
retry park retry park
park park retry retry
retry park park retry

questions.q: A job fails on every attempt. What does this print?
questions.explain: attempts: 3 means three tries in total, and context.attemptNumber counts from 1. After the third failure the job moves to the dead-letter store, which keeps the number of attempts and the last error's message as the reason.
options: [ 1, 2, 3 ] 3 mail provider timed out
[ 1 ] 1 mail provider timed out
[ 0, 1, 2 ] 3 mail provider timed out
[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] 4 mail provider timed out

questions.q: Only the email consumer fails at first. With one retry loop per consumer, what does this print?
questions.explain: Each consumer has its own retry state, so only email is tried again, and it succeeds on the third try. Re-publishing the whole event three times would have run audit and analytics three times too.
options: { email: 3, audit: 1, analytics: 1 }
{ email: 3, audit: 3, analytics: 3 }
{ email: 2, audit: 1, analytics: 1 }
{ email: 4, audit: 1, analytics: 1 }

questions.q: Finish handleOnce(consumer, eventId, work). It must run work() only the first time a given consumer sees a given event id, returning "done", and return "duplicate" afterwards. Different consumers are independent. If work() throws, the event must not count as processed, so a retry can run it again (rethrow the error).
questions.explain: Claim before the work (so a concurrent duplicate sees the claim), and release the claim when the work fails. That is what one database transaction gives you for free: the claim row and the work commit or roll back together.
questions.expected:
done, duplicate, done, db down, done
1 12

questions.q: payment.received v1 had { orderId, amountNaira } (a number of naira). Version 2 is { orderId, amount: { kobo, currency } }. Write upcastV1(payload) that returns the v2 shape: kobo is naira × 100 rounded to a whole number, and the currency is "NGN".
questions.explain: 0.29 * 100 is 28.999999999999996 in floating point, so Math.round is required, not Math.floor. An upcaster is a pure function from one shape to the next; it only uses data the old payload really has.

questions.q: Write the contract parser parseOrderCreated(payload). It returns the payload when orderId is a string starting with "ORD-", email is a string containing "@", and totalKobo is a positive safe integer. Otherwise it throws a TypeError whose message is order.created: invalid FIELD for the first invalid field in that order.
questions.explain: Optional chaining (payload?.orderId) makes null fail on the first field instead of crashing with a different error. Number.isSafeInteger rejects fractions of a kobo, which a money field must never hold.
questions.expected:
ok ORD-1
TypeError order.created: invalid orderId
TypeError order.created: invalid email
TypeError order.created: invalid totalKobo
TypeError order.created: invalid orderId

questions.q: Finish relay(outbox, publish). It walks the rows whose published is false in seq order, calls publish(row) (which returns { failed }), marks the row published only when failed is 0, and stops at the first failure to keep the order. It returns how many rows it published.
questions.explain: Sort by seq, because the array order is not the order the events were written. The first run publishes evt-2, fails on evt-3 and never tries evt-4. The second run picks up exactly where the first stopped.

questions.q: Write handleFailure(error, attempt, maxAttempts). Return "park" when error.serviceCode is one of MAILBOX_NOT_FOUND or INVALID_PHONE (permanent, whatever the attempt). Otherwise return "retry" while attempt is below maxAttempts, and "dead-letter" on the last attempt.
questions.explain: Permanent failures skip the retries and go straight to a person. Transient ones are retried until the attempts run out and then dead-lettered. Both end in the same visible place; only the time it takes to get there differs.

questions.q: Write subscribe(bus, contract, handler) for @zudojs/events. It subscribes to contract.type and calls handler with the payload after contract.parse(payload). A payload that fails the parser must not reach the handler.
questions.explain: The contract chooses both the event name and the payload type, so the handler's parameter type is derived, not claimed. The parser throws inside the bus handler, so a bad payload is recorded as a failed delivery with a clear cause, and your handler never sees it.
questions.expected:
reorder RICE-50KG, 3 left
failed: 1 stock.low: invalid payload

questions.q: Write readEvent(envelope, upcasters, latest). It throws a RangeError with the message vN is newer than this code when envelope.version is above latest. Otherwise it applies upcasters[v] for every version from envelope.version up to latest - 1, in order, and returns the resulting payload.
questions.explain: An event already at the latest version passes through untouched, because the loop runs zero times. Refusing newer versions keeps old code from guessing at a shape it does not know.

questions.q: Write revenueByDay(deliveries). Each delivery is { id, day, totalKobo }, and the list contains duplicate deliveries (same id). Count each event once and return an object mapping each day to its total in kobo.
questions.explain: Deduplicate by event id, not by the values: two different orders can have the same day and the same total. This is the analytics consumer in miniature; in the database the Set is the processed_events table.
